claims.text: The starting material is additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 with an fcc matrix.
The starting material is homogeneous and fine-grained, with minimal pre-existing grain-boundary precipitates.
During oxidizing exposure, Ti and Cr preferentially oxidize at grain boundaries.
The preferentially formed Ti- and Cr-containing grain-boundary oxides are brittle precipitates.
Grain-boundary oxide precipitates weaken intergranular cohesion and act as stress concentrators.
Oxide-induced boundary weakening promotes microcrack initiation, coalescence, and catastrophic intergranular fracture.
Under reducing conditions, insufficient formation of a protective oxide permits diffusion-driven segregation of reactive elements at grain boundaries.
Elemental segregation under reducing conditions undermines grain-boundary integrity and can initiate catastrophic failure.
Oxygen-rich exposure will produce thicker and more continuous grain-boundary oxide layers than are present in the unexposed state.
Oxygen-rich exposure will increase microcrack density relative to the unexposed state.
Oxygen-rich exposure will reduce failure strain, ductility, and toughness relative to the unexposed state.
Reducing exposure will produce detectable grain-boundary elemental segregation.
The amount of grain-boundary segregation under reducing conditions will correlate with loss of mechanical performance.
Both oxidizing and reducing exposures will cause catastrophic failure at lower applied loads than in the unexposed state.
Exposure at 800–1000 °C for 2–4 hours is sufficient to develop the proposed surface and intergranular modifications.
The unexposed alloy has minimal grain-boundary oxide or segregation and exhibits ductile failure in standard mechanical testing.
